common_name: Hot Chocolate Calla Lily (Rich Brown with Ruby-Red Overtones)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes after last frost in rich, moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; Hot Chocolate bears rich brown trumpet-shaped spathes warmed with ruby-red overtones.

directions: Plant rhizomes after the danger of frost has passed in fertile, evenly moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade. Hot Chocolate produces unusual, richly saturated brown spathes touched with ruby-red overtones above large, glossy, heart-shaped leaves generously spotted with white, making both the bloom and the foliage a striking cut-flower and border feature. It flowers over a long season from early summer into early fall on an interspecific hybrid that combines vigor with an unusual color palette. In zones 8-10 the rhizomes can overwinter in the ground with good drainage, while in colder regions they should be lifted before hard frost and stored dry over winter like dahlia tubers.

common_name: Cameo Calla Lily (Peach-Salmon with Dark Brown Eye)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes after last frost in rich, moist soil in full sun; Cameo bears long-lasting peach to salmon-orange spathes centered with a dark brown eye.

directions: Plant rhizomes after last frost in fertile, consistently moist soil in full sun, where Cameo produces long-lasting peach to salmon-orange trumpet-shaped spathes marked with a distinctive dark brown eye at the base. The mid-green, arrow-shaped leaves are lightly spotted white and set off the soft-colored blooms from summer into fall. As a marginal aquatic, Cameo tolerates boggy soil and can even be grown in submerged baskets at the edge of a pond in up to a foot of water, making it a versatile choice for both borders and water gardens. Lift and store the rhizomes dry over winter in climates colder than zone 8.

common_name: Best Gold Calla Lily (Deep Golden Yellow)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes after last frost in compost-enriched, moisture-retentive soil in full sun to part sun; Best Gold bears deep golden-yellow spathes on a compact plant.

directions: Plant rhizomes after last frost in compost-enriched, moisture-retentive soil in full sun to part sun, watering regularly through the growing season. Best Gold, selected from the yellow-flowered species Zantedeschia pentlandii, is a compact hybrid bearing deep golden-yellow spathes from midsummer into fall on a plant noticeably shorter than most colored calla hybrids. Its bright color and modest size make it well suited to container culture and the front of a mixed border, and it reliably draws butterflies and hummingbirds while being largely ignored by deer. In zones colder than 8, lift the rhizomes before frost and store them dry over winter.

common_name: Dark Eyes Calla Lily (Lavender-Pink with Maroon Eye)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes after last frost in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun; Dark Eyes bears lavender-pink chalices marked with a dark maroon patch at the base.

directions: Plant rhizomes after last frost in rich, moist, well-drained soil in partial shade to full sun, siting it where hot afternoon sun will not scorch the foliage. Dark Eyes, a Golden State Bulb introduction, sends up solid green, unspotted leaves in late spring topped by soft lavender-pink chalice-shaped spathes, each marked at its base with a dark maroon patch that gives the cultivar its name. This subtler, bicolor pastel effect distinguishes it from the more brightly colored calla hybrids and works well in mixed plantings with cool-toned perennials. In zones 8-10 rhizomes may be left in the ground through a mild winter, while in colder climates they should be lifted and stored dry like dahlia tubers.

planting.note: Plant rhizomes after last frost in rich, moist soil in full sun; Odessa bears glossy, almost-black purple chalice-shaped spathes on white-flecked foliage.

directions: Plant rhizomes after last frost in fertile, evenly moist, well-drained soil in full sun, where Odessa produces an abundance of glossy, dark purple spathes so deeply colored they read as near-black yet still catch a gleaming sheen in summer sunlight. Arrow-shaped, dark green leaves lightly flecked with white surround each flower stalk, providing a clean backdrop for the dramatic blooms from summer into fall. The dark, glossy spathes hold up exceptionally well as cut flowers, and the plant is generally left alone by deer and rabbits. In zones colder than 8, treat Odessa as an annual or lift the rhizomes before frost and store them dry over winter.
